Regarding the need for device updates, Mather acknowledged that while some legacy devices cannot be upgraded, the scale of legacy infrastructure in the United States may not require the massive retrofit undertaken in Germany, as natural equipment turnover provides opportunities for gradual modernization, though managing interactions between old and new devices remains a significant challenge. 1.3.4 Commercial Buildings Research Infrastructure and Behind-the-Meter Storage : Flexible and Modular Platforms for Building and Grid Research(Donald Price, NLR) In this presentation, Donald Price from NLR’s Building Technologies and Science center outlined the Commercial Buildings Research Infrastructure (CBRI) (NREL 2025) Behind-the-Meter Storage (BTMS) platforms designed to address the growing complexity of building-grid interactions. Research has emphasized that buildings represent the largest electrical load on the grid, and with the increasing installation of Distributed Energy Resources (DER) like Electric Vehicles (EV) and PV within buildings, there is a critical need for integrated research platforms to investigate intelligent efficiency, advanced controls, interoperability, demand flexibility, and energy storage systems. The CBRI platform provides a flexible research infrastructure with electrical capacity for three commercial buildings (400 Amps (A)/326 kilowatts (kW) each), utilizing Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) functionality to create a modular system that connects building simulation with buildings hardware such as Building Management Systems (BMS), Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) equipment, and various DERs. The platform features sophis- ticated emulation capabilities including up to 2-MW generation source emulation, dynamic air-side and water-side condition modeling for HVAC equipment, and connections to electric vehicle chargers exceeding 350 kW. A key in- novation is the HIL network that serves as a data streaming service connecting hardware and simulation components, enabling researchers to test grid-interactive efficient building technologies in controlled yet realistic environments. The BTMS component focuses on optimal design and control of behind-the-meter storage systems, combining ther- mal storage (560 kilowatt-hour (kWh) thermal capacity) with electrochemical storage (40 kWh lithium-ion battery) to investigate the optimal combination of these technologies. Integration experiments use HIL simulation with actual laboratory hardware to calibrate models and implement supervisory controls in realistic operational environments. During the discussion, Price addressed significant cybersecurity concerns, confirming multiple instances of power grid hacking by both state and non-state actors. The discussion revealed that many existing building control systems, some only 6-7 years old, already face obsolescence issues with outdated software and hardware lacking adequate cybersecurity protections.
